topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines disposable income?
options: Income available to households to spend or save after direct taxes
Total national output divided by the population
Income remaining after all spending has taken place
The wage a worker is paid before any deductions
questions.why: Disposable income is what determines whether customers can actually afford the product.
whyNot: That is GDP per capita.
That is discretionary or residual income.
That is gross pay, before tax.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines ease of doing business?
options: How straightforward it is to establish and run a business in a country
How cheap labour is in a country
How large a country's consumer market is
How stable a country's exchange rate is
questions.why: It covers registration, permits, contract enforcement, taxation and the ability to repatriate profit.
whyNot: That is a cost factor.
That is market size.
That is exchange rate stability.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Which of the following best defines political stability?
options: The likelihood that a country's government, laws and policies remain predictable over an investment's life
The number of political parties in a country
The frequency of elections in a country
The level of government spending as a share of GDP
questions.why: Predictability is what matters, and it matters far more for FDI than for exporting.
whyNot: The number of parties does not determine stability.
Regular elections can accompany high stability.
That is a fiscal measure.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Which factor determines whether a business can physically reach customers in a market?
options: Infrastructure
Disposable income
Political stability
The exchange rate
questions.why: Roads, ports, power, telecommunications and payment systems determine distribution cost and whether the customer can pay.
whyNot: Income determines affordability, not reach.
Stability affects risk, not physical distribution.
The exchange rate affects price competitiveness.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Why does the growth rate of income usually matter more than the level?
options: A business entering a market is buying its future rather than its present
Growth rates are easier to measure than income levels
The level of income does not affect affordability
Growth rates are always more stable than income levels
questions.why: A modest income growing quickly can support a product within a few years that it cannot support today.
whyNot: Both are measured routinely.
The level determines current affordability, which matters too.
Growth rates are typically more volatile.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: A country has GDP per capita of $6,400 growing at 6%. What does this most usefully tell a business?
options: The number of customers who can afford its product is growing quickly
All households in the country can afford its product
The country's total market is larger than a developed economy's
Its production costs there will be low
questions.why: The figure has to be linked to the specific product and to the segment that can afford it.
whyNot: An average says nothing about how many households reach that level.
Total market size depends on population as well.
Income data concerns the market, not production costs.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Why does income elasticity of demand matter in assessing a market?
options: A product with high income elasticity gains disproportionately from rising incomes
It determines the exchange rate the business will receive
It measures how quickly the population is growing
It sets the tariff rate on the product
questions.why: A luxury good benefits far more from income growth than a necessity does.
whyNot: Elasticity is unrelated to exchange rates.
That is population growth.
Tariffs are set by government.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Which of the following is an infrastructure problem that would rule out a perishable product?
options: Weak cold-chain facilities
A low level of card payment penetration
Slow company registration procedures
A volatile exchange rate
questions.why: Without refrigerated storage and transport the product cannot reach the customer in saleable condition.
whyNot: Payment penetration affects how customers pay, not product condition.
Registration delay is an ease-of-doing-business issue.
Currency volatility is a pricing and planning problem.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Why can a business's addressable market be far smaller than a country's population?
options: Infrastructure and income may only support the product in a few cities
Populations are always overstated in official data
Only urban residents are permitted to buy imported products
National averages exclude the wealthiest households
questions.why: A country may have good infrastructure in two cities and little elsewhere, so the addressable market is those cities.
whyNot: Population data is broadly reliable.
No such restriction generally exists.
Averages include all income.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Why does political stability matter more for a production location than for an export sale?
options: FDI commits assets that cannot be moved, while exporting can be stopped
Exporters pay higher taxes in unstable countries
Political risk only affects manufacturing
Exporters are protected by the WTO from political risk
questions.why: Making that distinction between reversible and irreversible commitment is a strong evaluative point.
whyNot: Tax treatment is not the issue.
Political risk affects all activity.
The WTO does not insure against political risk.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Why can a large, fast-growing market still be unattractive?
options: Hostile five forces may mean little profit is available once you are in it
Large markets are always harder to reach physically
Growth always ends within two years
Fast-growing markets have low incomes by definition
questions.why: Market size and market profitability are different questions, and a growing market attracts entrants which erodes the margins that attracted them.
whyNot: Size does not determine physical accessibility.
Growth can persist for decades.
Many fast-growing markets have rising incomes.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Why are Porter's five forces usually worse for a foreign entrant than for the local incumbent?
options: It has weaker bargaining power with suppliers and distributors, no established brand and no local knowledge
Foreign entrants pay higher tariffs on all inputs
The five forces apply only to foreign businesses
Local incumbents are legally protected from competition
questions.why: The forces are not the same for every firm in the market, and they are usually harsher for the newcomer.
whyNot: Tariffs depend on the goods, not on the firm's nationality.
They apply to all firms in an industry.
Legal protection of incumbents is unusual.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Which two issues should be distinguished when discussing exchange rates in a market assessment?
options: The level, which affects price competitiveness, and the volatility, which prevents planning
The spot rate and the interest rate
The official rate and the tax rate
The nominal rate and the population growth rate
questions.why: Saying which concern applies is what turns a mention of exchange rates into analysis.
whyNot: Interest rates are a separate variable.
Tax rates are unrelated to exchange rates.
Population growth is unrelated.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: Why is weak contract enforcement a serious concern for a market entrant?
options: A distributor who does not pay may be beyond practical recourse
It increases the tariff payable on imports
It prevents the business from advertising
It makes the exchange rate more volatile
questions.why: Restrictions on repatriating profit are a related concern: the returns cannot be brought home.
whyNot: Tariffs are unrelated to contract law.
Advertising is governed by separate regulation.
Contract enforcement does not drive currency movements.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: For a small island economy, what usually causes a market assessment to fail?
options: Population size and distribution cost rather than income level
Income levels being too low to support any product
The absence of any political stability
The impossibility of registering a business
questions.why: Total market value is income per head multiplied by population, and moving goods between islands is expensive and slow.
whyNot: Income per head may be relatively high.
Stability must be assessed on evidence, not assumed absent.
Registration is possible in such economies.

questions.topicTitle: Assessment of a country as a market
questions.stem: What is the correct order of work in a market assessment answer?
options: Rank the factors by importance for this product, then apply the data, then apply Porter, then judge
List the five factors in the order given in the specification, then conclude
Apply Porter first and ignore the five factors
State the recommendation first and then justify it with any available data
questions.why: For a perishable product infrastructure comes first; for a luxury good income distribution comes first.
whyNot: A fixed order with no ranking cannot reach the top band.
Both are needed: one for size, one for profitability.
A recommendation with no prior analysis is unsupported.
